tldr: By replacing raw step-by-step action sequence prediction with B-spline coefficient prediction, this paper achieves smooth motion generation and longer-horizon execution, delivering both high inference efficiency and high success rates in VLA models.
hero_caption: Architecture comparison between standard VLAs (left) and the proposed SMILE (right). By preserving the visual-language backbone and denoising core while replacing raw action outputs (Micro Actions) with B-spline coefficients (Macro Actions), the robot can smoothly execute longer horizons ($H$).
overview:
In Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robot control, action chunking is widely used to reduce inference cost: the model predicts a multi-step action sequence in a single call and executes a subset of those steps. Increasing the number of executed steps per call (the execution horizon $H$) amortizes the expensive VLA calls and speeds up inference.

However, conventional methods directly predict raw action sequences, which often contain high-frequency jitter and outliers. Extending the execution horizon $H$ accumulates these fluctuations, derailing the robot's trajectory and causing task success rates to plummet.

To tackle this dilemma, the authors introduce SMILE, an architecture-preserving interface that smooths action representations. Instead of predicting microscopic per-step actions independently, the model predicts the control points (coefficients) of a B-spline curve, which are decoded into a smooth trajectory using fixed basis functions.

In experiments across four distinct modern VLA models (SmolVLA, Evo1, VPP, and DAWN), SMILE substantially extended the execution horizon without increasing model scale across simulation environments (LIBERO, CALVIN) and a real-world platform (xArm7), simultaneously achieving faster inference and higher task success rates.
contributions: Proposed SMILE, an interface that performs denoising in a compact B-spline coefficient space to generate smooth trajectories and extend the execution horizon of VLAs.

Designed an architecture-preserving framework that replaces only lightweight input/output projection layers without altering backbones or conditioning paths, allowing easy integration into diverse VLAs.
Demonstrated accelerated inference, improved success rates, and dramatic reductions in acceleration and trajectory jitter across simulation (LIBERO, CALVIN) and real-world manipulation (xArm7).

sections.heading: Does Skimping on Inference Make Motion Erratic? The Long-Horizon VLA Dilemma
sections.summary: While action chunking speeds up inference by increasing the execution horizon $H$, accumulated motion jitter degrades task success. SMILE solves this issue by introducing a smooth action representation that predicts B-spline coefficients while preserving the underlying model architecture.
sections.details:
Calling a large multimodal VLA model at every control step is computationally prohibitive. Modern VLAs address this via action chunking: a single call predicts control inputs for multiple future steps, and the robot executes the first $H$ steps before taking a new observation. Increasing this execution horizon $H$ amortizes expensive model inference over more control steps, significantly cutting effective latency.

However, there is a catch. Predicting in raw action space often injects high-frequency jitter, abrupt directional shifts, and outliers into the chunk. When executing only 1–2 steps, the robot can correct course on the next call; over a longer horizon, these errors accumulate and lead to unintended behavior. Indeed, baselines like SmolVLA and Evo1 show steep drops in success rates as $H$ increases.

To address this, the authors propose SMILE (Smooth Motion for Improved Long-Horizon VLA Execution). Rather than predicting per-step controls independently, it predicts the coefficients (control points) of B-spline curves and deterministically decodes them into executable robot action sequences using a fixed basis.

Crucially, SMILE is architecture-preserving: it leaves the core vision-language feature extractor and denoising backbones (diffusion models or flow matching) untouched. Swapping only lightweight input/output layers allows robots to safely run longer execution horizons $H$ without increasing model parameters.

sections.heading: At the Crossroads of Chunking and Splines: Where SMILE Fits In
sections.summary: Prior work focused on chunk selection, asynchronous execution, or general-purpose tokenizers, whereas SMILE focuses on improving motion quality itself under synchronous fixed-horizon execution. It uniquely preserves diverse vision-conditioned VLA backbones as-is.
sections.details:
This section organizes related work into three streams to clarify SMILE's position:

- Action Chunking and Efficient Execution: Prior methods (such as BID, AAC, and AutoHorizon) select better chunks from candidate sets or dynamically adapt execution horizons. However, they do not alter the underlying action representation learned by the model. In contrast, SMILE replaces the action representation itself with compact B-spline coefficients.

- Smooth Action Representations and Real-Time Control: Works maintaining trajectory continuity include asynchronous prediction methods (RTC, ABPolicy), frequency-domain compression (FAST), and spline-based approaches (BEAST). SMILE distinguishes itself by focusing on the accuracy-efficiency trade-off of extending fixed execution horizons in synchronous control, designed as a lightweight interface for VLAs.

- Denoising Action Experts and Diverse Visual Architectures: Modern VLAs extend beyond standard VLM-centric designs to include video-prediction features (VPP) and explicit pixel motion (DAWN). SMILE is architecture-agnostic, retaining original perception and prediction modules while updating only the action-generation interface.

sections.heading: Why Extending Horizons Fails—and How SMILE Restores Stability
sections.summary: Existing raw-action models suffer sharp accuracy drops simply by extending the horizon $H$. In contrast, SMILE drastically reduces dropped objects and collisions even at long horizons, highlighting the importance of temporally smooth structure.
sections.details:
The authors first tested whether simply increasing the execution horizon $H$ yields efficiency gains. Lowering inference frequency naturally decreases per-step computation time, but forces the robot to operate in local open-loop control for longer intervals without new sensory input.

Empirical results confirmed that baseline models predicting raw actions suffer sharp performance degradation as $H$ grows. Simply stretching the horizon without addressing low-quality predicted action chunks leads to failure.

In contrast, SMILE maintained high success with long fixed horizons even in real-world, obstacle-heavy xArm environments, significantly cutting object drops and obstacle collisions. This indicates that gripper commands remain stable and arm trajectories stay steady from approach to transport. These observations lead to the conclusion that successful long-horizon execution fundamentally requires improving the temporal smoothness of predicted chunks.

sections.heading: Zero Backbone Changes: How SMILE Predicts and Decodes B-Spline Coefficients
sections.summary: SMILE predicts an action sequence of generation length $F$ as B-spline control points rather than raw values. A deterministic decoder reconstructs cumulative poses and uses finite differencing to produce actions fully compatible with standard robot controllers.
sections.details:
SMILE's core design is simple yet tailored to robotic control:

- Overview: Standard action experts output raw chunks of length $F$. SMILE instead predicts B-spline coefficients $M_j$ corresponding to translation, rotation, and gripper states. A fixed B-spline basis $\Phi_F^{(P, K)}$ (degree $P$, $K$ control points) deterministically decodes them into a smooth sequence, and the first $H$ steps are executed.

- B-Spline Representation and Decoding: From predicted control points, the decoder reconstructs cumulative translation $P_s$, cumulative rotation $R_s$ in command space, and continuous gripper trajectory $G_s$. Translation actions are computed via finite differences of cumulative positions: $a^{\mathrm{tr}}_{s,\tau} = P_s(\tau) - P_s(\tau-1)$. For rotation, cumulative rotation vectors are mapped to $SO(3)$ rotation matrices, relative rotations between adjacent steps are computed, and converted back into rotation vectors. Gripper values are used directly as absolute commands. This yields temporally cohesive, smooth control signals without modifying the robot's existing controller interface. Default settings use cubic splines ($P=3$) with $K=8$ control points.

- Architecture-Preserving Training Objective: The base model's noise schedule (diffusion or flow matching) remains identical; only the target is changed from raw actions to normalized spline coefficients $\Theta_{s,\mathrm{norm}}^{m,\star}$. The loss is a weighted sum of squared errors across modalities (translation, rotation, gripper) with equal weighting ($\lambda=1$).

- Target Coefficient Construction: Target training trajectories are extracted as length-$F$ native actions from existing datasets, converted to cumulative trajectories, and uniquely mapped to target coefficients via least squares against the fixed basis matrix $\Phi_F$.

sections.heading: From Simulation to Real Robots: Gaining Speed and Success While Slashing Jitter
sections.summary: Evaluations on LIBERO, CALVIN, and a real-world xArm7 showed consistent gains in success rates and inference efficiency across SmolVLA, Evo1, VPP, and DAWN. At matched horizons, within-chunk acceleration dropped by ~79%, demonstrating dramatic smoothing.
sections.details:
Experiments covered two simulation benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation:

- LIBERO Benchmark: Evaluated on SmolVLA and Evo1. SMILE-Evo1 improved success rate from 92.7% to 98.0% while expanding the horizon from 14 to 16, cutting per-action inference time from 8.5ms to 8.0ms. SmolVLA saw even larger gains: extending $H=1$ to $H=10$ raised success from 74.0% to 82.6% while speeding up inference by roughly 10.1x (243.9ms down to 24.2ms). Gains were particularly prominent on the error-sensitive 'LIBERO-Long' suite.

- CALVIN Benchmark: In this multi-task setup requiring 5 consecutive subtasks, SMILE was applied to video-predictive VPP and explicit pixel-motion DAWN. Both models extended $H$ from 10 to 15, lowering inference time (SMILE-VPP went from 19.1ms to 13.0ms) while raising the average completed sequence length (SMILE-VPP reached 4.42 vs. baseline 4.33, approaching DreamVLA at roughly 15x the inference speed).

- Real-Robot Experiments (xArm7): Tasks required picking a specified fruit and placing it into a basket in Plain and Cluttered settings. In Cluttered settings, SMILE-Evo1 boosted success from 8.3% to 56.7%, and SMILE-VPP from 70.8% to 88.3%. Unintended contacts (Hit) and misgrasps dropped sharply, and mid-transport drops seen in the baselines dropped to zero with SMILE.

- Smoothness Analysis and Ablations: Comparing SmolVLA at a matched $H=10$, SMILE reduced non-boundary within-chunk acceleration by 78.6% and velocity sign-change rate (jitter) by 42.3%. Ablations confirmed that $K=8$ control points with cubic splines ($P=3$) provided the best balance of flexibility and performance.

sections.heading: Wrap-Up: Changing the Representation Makes VLAs Faster and Smoother
sections.summary: By shifting action generation to a B-spline coefficient space while preserving model backbones, SMILE overcomes the trade-off between accuracy and efficiency in long-horizon VLA execution. It represents a versatile approach across diverse models and real-world hardware.
sections.details:
This paper highlights the limitations of predicting per-step raw actions and introduces SMILE, a novel interface for predicting and decoding compact B-spline coefficients.

Ensuring temporal consistency and smoothness within chunks prevents trajectories from breaking down even under longer fixed execution horizons $H$. Consequently, amortized inference latency per action is reduced while boosting task success rates.

SMILE delivered consistent improvements across four distinct architectures—VLM-centric, video-predictive, and pixel-motion-guided models—and validated its efficacy in both simulation and real-world manipulation. It stands as a practical, high-impact framework showing that inference efficiency and control quality can be elevated simply by rethinking action representations without redesigning massive model backbones.

takeaways: To accelerate VLA inference via action chunking, smoothing the action representation to extend the execution horizon is far more effective than simply scaling the model.
Predicting B-spline control points allows seamless integration into existing VLA backbones by replacing only linear input/output layers.
Smooth motion generation directly translates to real-world benefits: fewer obstacle collisions and elimination of dropped objects during transport.
limitations: The execution horizon $H$ remains fixed within each episode, without integration into adaptive horizon frameworks that dynamically adjust replanning frequencies during abrupt disturbances.
The spline basis (cubic splines with 8 control points) is chosen heuristically, which may limit expressiveness for extremely complex or discontinuous motions, such as sudden contact impacts.
